job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Erik Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight, make coffee in my sister Lena's kitchen and spend the morning on applications. I rent her spare room for a fair price, because she says family or not, she has her own rent to pay. In the afternoon I'm either at a library desk or tutoring two school kids in maths, which brings in a little. I finished economics and finance at Kellerby University in June, top of the year, and my thesis was on why rents outrun wages. Internships at the Harbour Credit Union and a bank's back office taught me how the money actually moves. Since then it's been fifty-odd applications and two interviews that went nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the sensible outcome, since we'd all get time to adjust. To my friends I'd say the loud predictions were used to justify cuts that were going to happen anyway. Online I'd probably share something about how short-term profit targets drive hiring, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried regardless. I owe 38,000 and my savings wouldn't cover three weeks of rent. A plateau doesn't make more junior finance jobs appear in Harrow Bay, where there are maybe four employers who take graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, and I'd widen to jobs two hours away that I could commute to or move for. I'd put all the tutoring income towards the rent and the loan, and I'd ask Lena whether I could stay on through winter. I'd also add one or two jobs in credit unions and housing finance, which match my thesis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, honestly. Not scared of the technology, scared of the calendar, because each month of silence makes my CV look staler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the two interviews that went nowhere tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both interviews said I was strong but they'd chosen a candidate with a year of experience. It showed me the real barrier is experience, not skill. A firm that wants a year of experience for a trainee role isn't really offering a trainee role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI is mostly hype, what do you think holds back hiring right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shareholders and the way firms are run. They'd rather keep one tired manager doing two jobs than hire a junior and train them, because the training pays off later and the quarter ends soon. I'd back rules or tax breaks that reward firms that train.

say: The loud AI predictions gave firms an excuse for cuts that were happening **anyway**.
Short-term profit targets drive hiring more than **technology** does.
think: I'm worried regardless: 38,000 owed and savings that cover **three weeks** of rent.
Harrow Bay has maybe four employers who take **graduates**.
do: Keep applying and widen the search to jobs **two hours** away.
Put all the tutoring money to **rent** and loan payments.
Target credit unions and housing finance, which match my **thesis**.
feel: **Flat**, afraid of the calendar more than of the technology.
S0.quote: A firm that wants a year of experience for a trainee role isn't really offering a trainee role.
fieldNote: Blames **shareholders** and short-term management, not machines, and wants incentives for training.
Calm in tone but his money and the lack of local employers keep him **anxious**.
Sees the experience trap clearly, which shapes where he applies.

steps.text: Apply to jobs within two hours of Harrow Bay
Target credit unions and housing finance teams that fit my thesis
Put all tutoring income towards rent and the loan
Ask Lena to let me keep the spare room through winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we can't pretend otherwise, but who gets the benefit is a political choice. At work or online I'd argue for training funds paid for by the firms that save money. People shouldn't be left to retrain on their own credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my kind of job is one of the first to feel it. Credit unions and banks are already putting loan checks through software, and the back office where I interned was told to stop replacing people who left. It means fewer trainee seats at exactly the time I'm applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools rather than dabble, since the firms that do still hire will want someone who can supervise them. I'd take a short data analysis course, probably evenings, and build one small project on rent data that I can show. And I'd apply for roles that mix finance with talking to members or customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit impatient. I'm ready to change, but I can't tell which change is the right one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used AI tools now and then. What work did it do well for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was good at tidying my cover letters and summarising a long annual report in a minute. It was bad at the numbers when I checked its sums. That said, if I can spot the bad sums, a firm needs someone like me to check, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses most when entry-level roles shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones at the start, like me, and the people in the back office who aren't managers. Senior staff keep their jobs and call it efficiency. I'd want a levy on firms that cut entry-level hiring and put the money into traineeships.

say: It's real, but who gets the benefit is a **political** choice.
Firms that save money should pay into **training funds**, not leave people to retrain alone.
think: Banks and credit unions already push loan checks through **software**, shrinking trainee seats.
The back office I interned in stopped **replacing** people who left.
do: Get properly good at **AI tools** instead of dabbling, so I can supervise them.
Take an evening **data analysis** course and build a project on rent data.
Apply for roles that mix finance with talking to **members**.
feel: **Impatient** and uneasy: ready to change, unsure which change.
S1.quote: Credit unions and banks are already putting loan checks through software, and the back office where I interned was told to stop replacing people who left.
fieldNote: Moves from analysis to a practical plan, typical of his **steady** style.
Wants a levy on firms cutting entry-level jobs, so his politics shows up in his fix.
Tested the tools himself, so he speaks from **evidence** not rumour.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant daily to check and draft finance work
Take an evening data analysis course and build a rent data project
Apply for credit union roles that include member contact
Back a levy on firms that cut entry-level hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency action, now, and I'd say it publicly. Governments should put a floor under incomes and slow down any cuts until there's a plan. I'd be posting that and going to meetings, because quiet people lose out in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be frightened. My whole training is a thinking-work career and I'd have two years to get into it before it stops being a career. I think I'd probably never get a full finance job, and I'd be paying the loan on a wage from something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd ask the loan servicer what happens to the debt if incomes collapse, and push them for a payment pause. I'd move into jobs that need hands or presence, maybe in care or at a housing co-op where I could use my money knowledge. I'd keep the tutoring because kids will still need people. And I'd go to every town meeting where this is discussed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. Like everyone is told to jump and nobody has told us where the ground is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What do you do with your loan, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to pause it, but I wouldn't count on it. If I can't, I'd cut everything except rent and food and put any earnings aside, since I couldn't trust the future income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Lena, who's a dental receptionist and would lose that to software. And my parents, who run a small shop and have no pension to speak of. I'd move back in with them if their shop closed, and that would be a defeat I can already feel.

say: Governments need to put a **floor** under incomes and slow cuts until there's a plan.
Quiet people lose out in a crisis, so I'd be **loud**.
think: I'd have two years to get a finance **career** before it stops being one.
I'd probably never get a full finance job and pay the loan from **other** work.
do: Ask the loan servicer what happens if incomes collapse and push for a **pause**.
Move toward work needing presence, like care or a **housing co-op**.
Keep **tutoring** and attend every town meeting on the subject.
feel: **Dizzy**: told to jump when nobody has said where the ground is.
S2.quote: Everyone is told to jump and nobody has told us where the ground is.
fieldNote: Fear is wide: for himself, his sister Lena and his parents' small **shop**.
Switches from tool-user to organiser, which fits his political outlook.
Plans around presence-based work, understanding the three-year **robot** gap.

steps.text: Ask the loan servicer for a payment pause
Look for care or housing co-op roles that use money skills
Go to town meetings and press for an income floor
Cut everything except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it to build the safety net. I'd talk to friends about unions for young finance workers and about public retraining. I'd also quietly tell them to pay down debt now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I can get one proper job and some skills before it hits. What worries me is the second half of that sentence, where the job disappears around 2031 and I've got a mortgage-sized debt and no plan. I'd rather sort the plan out now than leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue any finance role in the next year, because the experience counts, and I'd pay at least 500 a month at the loan. In the second and third year I'd learn data analysis and AI auditing, something where someone checks the machine. I'd save a cushion of six months of rent, so a bad year doesn't wipe me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Five years feels like seeing the storm on the radar instead of feeling the first drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change your move on the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me clear a chunk of it, maybe a third. That cuts what I owe if the state doesn't help, and it also shows I'm serious about being a reliable borrower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents' shop to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to pay off their loan on the shop premises and keep a bit more cash. I'd also help them learn the stock and billing tools, so they don't pay someone else to run it for them.

say: Five years is a **window** to build the safety net, including public retraining.
I'd talk to friends about **unions** for young finance workers.
think: I can get one proper job and some **skills** before it hits, but then the job may vanish around 2031.
I'd rather sort the **plan** now than leave it.
do: Take any finance role in the next year and pay at least **500** a month at the loan.
Learn data analysis and **AI auditing**, where a person checks the machine.
Build a **six-month** cushion of rent money.
feel: **Better**, like seeing the storm on the radar before the first drops.
S3.quote: Five years feels like seeing the storm on the radar instead of feeling the first drops.
fieldNote: Uses extra time to turn **fear** into a three-year plan with figures.
Spans family: wants his parents to clear their own **loan** and learn the shop tools.
Still expects a bad end in 2031 and prepares for it rather than denying it.

steps.text: Take the first finance job offered and learn the firm's systems
Pay at least 500 a month at the student loan
Learn data analysis and AI auditing in years two and three
Help my parents learn the shop's stock and billing tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and the real fight is about who owns the gains. I'd argue for shorter working weeks and public ownership of some of the new wealth. I'd say it at work, if I had one, and in union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly secure, though not completely. In ten years I could be a decent analyst, and if the work changes shape I'd have the savings and the skills to move. I think I'd be alright, as long as I didn't stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job in finance, even a modest one, and learn on the job. I'd study part-time for a professional qualification and clear the loan in about six years. By year five I'd look at moving into something like policy analysis or housing finance that serves people directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I can see a path, and ten years is enough for mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay in finance for a few years, then look for a role in housing or public policy. Money knowledge is useful anywhere, and mixing it with people work seems the safest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cousin about picking a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to pick something where a person has to be in the room, and to learn how to ask a machine good questions. Don't choose a degree for the job title, choose it for what it lets you do.

say: Ten years is a long runway, and the real fight is over who **owns** the gains.
I'd argue for **shorter** working weeks and public ownership of some new wealth.
think: I feel fairly secure, as long as I don't **stand still**.
Money knowledge is useful anywhere, so I'd have **room** to move.
do: Take a modest first finance job and study part-time for a **qualification**.
Clear the loan in about **six years**.
By year five, move toward **policy analysis** or housing finance.
feel: Mostly **calm**: ten years is enough for mistakes.
S4.quote: Don't choose a degree for the job title, choose it for what it lets you do.
fieldNote: Time lets his steady nature work: **small** steps, no leaps.
Turns the question into one about who owns the gains, his political side.
His cousin advice shows he now sees **presence-based** work as safer.

steps.text: Take a modest first finance job and learn on the job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. I could cope with a slow squeeze, but not with everything falling at once while I owe this much. What would help is a payment pause on the loan, a public traineeship scheme, and firms that have to keep hiring juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe only that I don't want sympathy, I want a real way in. I'm ready to learn the tools and move house for it. I just need someone to open one door.

headlineQuote: I don't want sympathy, I want a real way in. I'm ready to learn the tools and move house for it.
portrait: Erik is 23, top of his economics and finance class, and lives in a **rented spare room** at his sister Lena's flat.
He owes 38,000 and has under a month of savings, plus tutoring income and fifty rejected applications.
Steady and evidence-minded, he tests tools, then **commits**, and blames shareholder short-termism over machines.
He gets calmer as time grows, from alarmed at two years to uneasy at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because he'd have two years and a large loan with no clear safety net.
whatWouldHelp: A **payment pause** on the student loan, a public traineeship scheme and firms obliged to keep hiring juniors.
